articles.title_orig: China’s Trade Surplus Nears $1 Trillion as Exports Surge
articles.title_zh: China’s Trade Surplus Nears $1 Trillion as Exports Surge
articles.content_orig:
China's economic growth accelerated to 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, as robust foreign demand for the country's technological goods largely offset drags from a deepening property slump and sluggish consumer demand.
Third-quarter growth beat Reuters-polled economists' expectation of a 4.4% expansion, and was also higher than the three-year low of 4.3% in the second quarter .
"The rebound in September salvaged the lukewarm performance in July and August," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, attributing the recovery to improved government investment that helped arrest the consistent worsening in fixed asset investment, an "ever-strong" external sector and a weak base. China's monthly trade surplus reached a record high of $133.5 billion .
Momentum from the three forces will likely extend into the fourth quarter, Xu said, forecasting a full-year growth rate of 4.7%.
The data shows an economy still leaning on factories and overseas buyers while households and private investors hold back, with growth through the first nine months averaging 4.6%, broadly in line with Beijing's official target range of 4.5% to 5%.
In September, retail sales eked out a 1.1% growth, exceeding analysts' forecast for 0.6% increase, while industrial output grew 5.5% from a year earlier, in line with the forecast of 5.5% growth. The urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2% in September.
For the first nine months this year, fixed asset investment in urban areas declined 7.2% from the same period a year earlier, compared with a 7.3% drop estimated in a Reuters poll. Investment channeled into real estate development deepened declines, falling 20.6% in the January to September period , compared with 19.9% in the first eight months.
"The prolonged housing slump will continue to limit the spillover from stronger industrial activity to the wider economy," Sheana Yue, senior economist at Oxford Economics, as Chinese households see their wealth stored in property shrink over the years.
Yue also dismissed the idea that green shoots have emerged in the property market, as home sales, construction starts, and prices offer little indication that the sector downturn is "bottoming out."
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as energy costs surge and its manufacturing and export surge has provoked growing anxiety among trading partners. Meanwhile, other pockets of the economy remain weak, weighed down by feeble consumption and a multiyear property slump.
"It is clear that domestic imbalances between supply and demand continue rising," Eswar Prasad, an economics professor at Cornell University, said in an emailed note after the data release on Monday. "The government might become more sanguine and maintain a passive approach, rather than infusing stimulus into the economy in tandem with much-needed reforms," he added.
Producer prices climbed at their fastest pace in over four years , rising 5% in September, while consumer inflation remains below 1%, reflecting persistent excess capacity and weak demand that are constraining businesses' pricing power. "This potentially leaves firms to absorb more of the cost shock through lower margins rather than higher selling prices," said Yue.
Economists largely expect the People's Bank of China to hold benchmark lending rates unchanged through this year, leaving fiscal measures to do most of the work.
While the decent growth pace may reduce the immediate pressure for Beijing to ramp up stimulus, Yue expects the implementation of already-announced measures to accelerate, supporting investment and activity in the coming quarters.
Chinese authorities have stepped up fiscal support in recent weeks, including a package of targeted rate cuts and mortgage subsidies in late September. Earlier this month, it also allocated 550 billion yuan of unused debt quota to help ease local government financial strains and bolster infrastructure spending.
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that quarterly GDP growth was 4.5%.

articles.title_orig: Rubio Confirms Talks Are Underway About Possible U.S.-China-Russia Summit On Ukraine War
articles.title_zh: Rubio Confirms Talks Are Underway About Possible U.S.-China-Russia Summit On Ukraine War
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report.
The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel on the global market.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters.
"The president is open to anything that he can do to help bring a war to an end, if it's possible, and we'll continue to look for opportunities to do that," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.
It comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. Over the past week, a series of moves by the Trump administration has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. It caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism from fellow Republicans.
Over the weekend, Trump defended his decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well as an executive order on Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump and Zelenskyy have traded criticism over how to end the war in Ukraine, with Trump accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace , while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia risks prolonging the conflict. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."
The tensions come as Russia launched another wave of overnight attacks on Ukraine, firing 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones across the country, according to Zelenskyy.
In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy said the strikes damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities, leaving at least 550,000 households without power. He also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the missile attacks. Casualties were reported, while a medical clinic, school, metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.
The latest move comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up diesel prices.
A so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Oct. 11 saw Moscow continuing strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure. Ukraine had then paused strikes for three days, but resumed attacks again last Thursday.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday.
On Sunday, he also told Bloomberg that "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate."
"I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."
Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukraine launching a strike of over 1,000 drones into Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Last week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military grade version of SpaceX's Starlink which it uses to control military forces and defend against Russian strikes.
Trump denied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."
The restrictions meant that platforms that traveled above 160 kilometers an hour (100 miles an hour), such as interceptor drones, had lost connectivity.
Ukrainian media reported Zelenskyy as saying that the restrictions were a "planned operation," as Ukraine had sent cars with Starlink to EU countries to test Starlink's connectivity, and discovered that there were no such restrictions in those countries.
Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
The Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Indonesia’s Selloff Deepens Across Stocks, Bonds on MSCI Risk
articles.title_zh: Indonesia’s Selloff Deepens Across Stocks, Bonds on MSCI Risk
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia's benchmark stock index plunged over 5% on Monday to its lowest level in six years, as concerns over a potential downgrade by MSCI intensified fears of further foreign investor outflows.
The Jakarta Composite Index tumbled to its lowest level since early October 2020, extending a bruising sell-off in Indonesian equities. MSCI, the index provider, on Friday proposed reclassifying Indonesia directly from an emerging market to stand-alone status, raising the prospect of the country's removal from major global equity benchmarks.
MSCI is expected to make a final decision by June, with the potential reclassification hinging on whether Indonesian authorities can demonstrate meaningful improvements in market governance and transparency.
Goldman Sachs warned in a Sunday note that a full removal from MSCI's emerging-market indexes could trigger approximately $5.6 billion in passive fund outflows, equivalent to 18 days of average daily trading volume for constituents of the MSCI Indonesia Investable Market Index.
An additional $2.7 billion could be at risk if FTSE Russell subsequently takes similar action, although the bank stressed that such a move would be a separate scenario.
Goldman estimated that active funds benchmarked to MSCI and FTSE indexes hold more than $8 billion in Indonesian equities, although any selling by these investors would be discretionary rather than automatically triggered by a downgrade.
The bank maintained its underweight rating on Indonesian equities, citing persistent index uncertainty, weak corporate earnings and macroeconomic headwinds.
"Valuations have compressed significantly, but remain above historical troughs; index, earnings, and macro risks constrain a re-rating," Goldman strategists led by Alvin So wrote.
The MSCI Indonesia Index has fallen 47% this year as of Friday, data provided by the bank showed, with foreign investors withdrawing a net $5.1 billion from Indonesian equities over the period.
Foreign ownership of Indonesian stocks has declined to 25% in October from 27% in January, while the value of foreign holdings has nearly halved to approximately $130 billion from $250 billion, the bank said.
Despite the steep declines, Goldman cautioned that Indonesian equities may not have bottomed. The MSCI Indonesia Index's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 7.3 times, its lowest level since the global financial crisis, but remains above historical troughs.
The strategists also expect Indonesia's central bank to raise interest rates twice more, by 25 basis points each in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027, potentially adding further pressure to economic growth and equity valuations.

articles.title_orig: Independent MP Helen Haines critically injured in attack near electorate office
articles.title_zh: Independent MP Helen Haines critically injured in attack near electorate office
articles.content_orig:
Australian lawmaker Helen Haines was in a critical condition on Monday after being deliberately struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, police and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.
Victoria Police said a 43-year-old man had been arrested after the attack on independent MP Haines inWangaratta, around three hours’ drive northeast of Melbourne.
Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital, Albanese said.
“All of our thoughts are with Helen, her family, her friends, her team, and her community at this extremely difficult time. We are praying for her full recovery,” Albanese told a press conference.
Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason told a press conference there was no further threat to the public.
Albanese said it was too early to determine the motive for the attack, though a terrorism taskforce would be investigating the arrested suspect.
“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response,” a statement by Haines’ family posted on her Facebook page said.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
articles.title_zh: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.
Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.
The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".
Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.
The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.
Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed.
In a post on social media, Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."
It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."
Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.
The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.
Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.
In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.
Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.
Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI , with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.
In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.
Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.
The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.
The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.
Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document , making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.
Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".

articles.title_orig: Police say 10 suspects arrested for West Bank settler attacks on journalist, EU diplomats
articles.title_zh: Police say 10 suspects arrested for West Bank settler attacks on journalist, EU diplomats
articles.content_orig:
Amid US pressure on a surge of settler violence in the occupied West Bank, Israeli police arrested at least 10 suspects in the weekend attacks on a Washington Post journalist and an entourage of European diplomats.
Police said the operation to locate and arrest the suspects was called “Olive Leaf,” an apparent reference to the recent start of the olive harvest in the West Bank, which has seen a dramatic rise in settler attacks.
On Friday, settlers attacked and hospitalized veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine as she traveled with a group of Palestinians at the start of the olive harvest. One day later, settlers attacked a group of European diplomats visiting the Palestinian Christian town of Taybeh.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee welcomed the arrests as a “very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine.”
According to police, security forces worked with the Israeli military to locate and arrest the suspects across the area with the attacks took place. “During this activity, 10 suspects were arrested, findings linking them to the incidents were sized and several vehicles were confiscated,” police said.
“We are working to collect evidence, findings and testimonies and to consolidate an evidentiary infrastructure that will enable bringing those involved to justice,” said Israel Police Superintendent Moshe Pinchi in a statement.
Israeli human rights group Yesh Din documented more than 530 incidents of settler violence since the beginning of the olive harvest in late-September, averaging 27 violent incidents each day. According to Yesh Din, Israeli soldiers were present at roughly one quarter of the attacks over this period.
On Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration has told Israel that the US “doesn’t want to see a new spark” in the West Bank and called on Israel to take action against settler violence.
“We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff,” said Rubio before his flight to India and Uzbekistan. “The President has been very clear. He’s said this repeatedly. He does not want to see friction or anything - a crisis - going on in the West Bank.”
Despite video of the attacks on both Levine, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has tried to cast doubt on the violence, saying afterwards that “serious questions remain.” In an apparent attempt to avoid upsetting his right-wing voter base so close to Israel’s elections, Netanyahu has repeatedly downplayed the severity and scale of settler violence, claiming it’s carried out by a rogue group.
Meanwhile, Israel’s defense minister said on Monday he would not reinstate administrative detention against Jewish Israelis, which allows authorities to hold suspects without charge or trial. The draconian measure was one of Israel’s most effective tools against settler extremism, but the defense minister cancelled its use against Jewish Israelis as one of his first decisions nearly two years ago.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election, which will take place on October 27, calling him “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant.” For weeks, Trump had sidestepped questions on whether Netanyahu should be re-elected, including just days earlier when he said, “I don’t trust anyone in the world of politics.”

articles.title_zh: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.content_orig:

Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
At least one person was killed and eight others injured after multiple waves of Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight on Oct. 19.
Several explosions rocked the capital just before 11 p.m., with further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m., Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported. Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said damage was reported in at least three districts.
One person was killed in the Desnianskyi District where a non-residential building caught fire and a metro station was damaged, DSNS said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko earlier reported a fatality was that of 21-year-old woman.
The above-ground Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were temporarily closed for repairs, city officials said.
Five people were injured in the Solomianskyi District when a 25-story residential building was damaged, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It is not yet clear where the other injuries occurred.
Photos of the damaged Cosmo Multimall shopping and entertainment center in the Solomianskyi District emerged on social media following the attack.
Klitschko also reported damage to a medical center in the same district. The blast wave shattered more than 200 windows, damaged doors and ceilings, and damaged medical equipment, he said.
No medical center staff were injured, and there were no patients inside the facility at the time of the attack.
Russian attacks also affected settlements in Kyiv Oblast surrounding the capital. In Irpin, located about 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Kyiv, 17 people were injured, including eight children. Search operations are ongoing, according to Tymur Tkachenko , head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration.
Tkachenko added that the attack damaged 84 properties in Irpin, including 70 houses, 4 high-rise buildings, and industrial and warehouse premises.
Recent ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv have arrived with little or no advance warning amid deteriorating relations between Ukraine and the U.S., which provides intelligence used to track Russian missile launches.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on the morning of Oct. 19 that Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, adding that Kyiv had received no advance warning from its partners about the launches.
According to Zelensky, Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region being the primary targets.
"When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners," Zelensky wrote on X.
"The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia's desire to drag this war out."
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Ukrainian Air Force's communications department, said on national television that Russia launched two waves of ballistic missile attacks overnight on Oct. 19, at around 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. local time.
Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners ahead of the first wave, but information about the second wave was provided, Ihnat said.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
"Information was indeed not provided the first time, for certain reasons. Our experts are looking into this together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred. Information was provided at 3 a.m.," Ihnat said.
Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Phone alerts went off moments before the blasts, while the street sirens began "howling during the explosions," Chief Editor Olga Rudenko reported.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first overnight wave followed a similar pattern.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened," the official said. "They're up to something again."
It can be common for Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles to hit with very little advance warning .
The attack came just hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky said the U.S. had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine about Russian missile launches.
The president's announcement came as a relief, after Kyiv endured "massive explosions" on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack came after the U.S. threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries, sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials have previously explained that satellite surveillance of launch sites can be vulnerable to transmission delays. Bad weather may also cause interference with the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellites, a surveillance network U.S. forces use to monitor Russian launch sites.
But the senior official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said this explanation was unlikely.
"This has never happened before ... but now we're seeing 'bad weather' three times in a row," the official said.
"When nothing comes through on any channel... well, we get it."
"A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia could help end the war sooner," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said. "A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."
Earlier, residents had little warning before the missiles struck. The explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The number includes 2,100 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Zelensky has appealed to Washington repeatedly, making the case for additional Patriot missiles as Russia intensifies strikes against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
"The trend this year continues," Zelensky said, "Since the start of fall, our warriors have liberated more territory than the Russians have managed to capture. The same was true at other points this year."
Trump appointee Scott Bessent insisted that no sanctions against Russia had been lifted — they had merely been waived.
"His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead."
"We are very thankful for this... Now it works," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
A flying object, likely a drone, entered Lithuanian airspace and exploded on Oct. 18, sending residents to shelters and damaging a civilian vehicle, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said.
According to the president, the U.S. and Ukraine are in "constant communication" and are preparing their "next steps in diplomacy."
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed the attack, reporting fires at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District.
The attackers attempted to set fire to satellite antennas and a control unit, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said.

articles.title_zh: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know

Gilets jaunes movement calls for further demonstrations in France as Giorgia Meloni schedules crisis talks after looting in Italian cities
Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after 2,400 arrests across France
There are no signs of French protests stopping anytime soon: the yellow vest movement, de gilets jaunes , has just announced a “second act” of protests for upcoming Saturday, 24 October – and then again a week after that, too.
The idea is to “keep the momentum going” until another major demonstration planned for 5 November, a group member told AFP.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni will hold a crisis meeting with top security officials on Monday after two days of ransacking and looting in Milan allegedly perpetrated by gangs of hooded youths.
The unrest began on Saturday on the fringes of a protest against the rising cost of living. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.
In Milan, more than 200 were detained by police, allegedly responsible for ransacking shops and smashing windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s Duomo. According to reports in the Italian press on Monday, 80% were minors, with many responding to appointments made on social media and sharing selfies as they bragged about the damage caused.
They were not believed to have been affiliated with any political party or organised groups or movements.
Meloni said on Saturday that the perpetrators were “thugs who exploit demonstrations to spread chaos, attack those who guarantee security, and hold entire cities to hostage”.
“To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not,” she wrote on X.
During her more than four years in power, Meloni has enacted tough security measures, including against peaceful protesters.
In July, her cabinet approved so-called “anti-maranza” legislation in response to a rise in child gangs and youth delinquency in city centres. “Maranza” is a slang term used to describe gangs of delinquent youths, usually coming from suburban areas.
Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.

Protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre museum in Paris in support of a nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”, the museum’s management and unions told AFP.
The museum could not open as scheduled because of a protest led by students from the Ecole du Louvre, management said. A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”
Back to France , the authorities in Marseille have just issued a ban of any public gatherings and demonstrations “throughout the entire commune” from midday to 8pm.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has responded to the latest wave of Russian attacks on Ukraine, confirming Ukraine had no prior warning from the US and seemingly accusing Washington of being in the state of denial about the reality of the war.
“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners, ” he said.
“They again targeted energy facilities and infrastructure, but a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and ordinary residential buildings were also damaged.”
Showing growing frustration with the attacks and continued criticism from US president Donald Trump , he said:
“ Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end. We have responded positively to EVERY ceasefire proposal. Russia’s response, time and again, has been ballistic missiles, “shaheds,” and killings.
Putin not only doesn’t want to end this war – he doesn’t even want to take any steps toward de-escalation. EVERY ONE of our partners has experienced this firsthand when they heard Russia’s refusals.
And it is crucial to call things what they are. To call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine defend lives. When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine’s air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners.
The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia’s desire to drag this war out.”

Footage showed police in riot gear firing teargas and using water cannon after several hundred hooded protesters smashed shop windows and set bins alight in the area around Piazza del Duomo in central Milan.
The clashes echoed scenes of violence in neighbouring France , where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.
Meanwhile, lorry drivers have caused widespread disruption across southern Italy, blocking major roads and creating huge traffic jams in Sicily, Puglia and Calabria in protest at the mounting financial pressure on the haulage industry.
Hundreds of petrol stations have run out of fuel, while supermarkets are beginning to report shortages of several products, particularly fresh food. Pharmacies have also been affected, raising concerns about disruption to essential supplies.
“We are asking the government to urgently convene a meeting with industry associations. Otherwise, we will consider a nationwide strike,” said Pasquale Russo, president of Conftrasporto, an association representing Italian haulage companies.
“The situation is very concerning because the excessive price increases affecting the haulage industry have created a highly tense situation among transport companies, leading to spontaneous protests in some areas of the country,” he added.
In several parts of southern Italy, petrol stations have run out of both petrol and diesel, with motorists facing long queues at the few filling stations still operating. The road blockades have also caused extensive traffic disruption, with fears growing that prolonged protests could further disrupt supplies of food, fuel and other essential goods.
French president Emmanuel Macron has declined interior minister Laurent Nuñez’s offer to resign after widespread riots over the weekend, despite “failures in anticipation and intelligence” that were deemed to worsen the crisis engulfing the country.

Saturday, one of the most violent days of unrest in years, left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country .

articles.title_orig: NHS bosses say smaller maternity units may have to close
articles.title_zh: NHS bosses say smaller maternity units may have to close
articles.content_orig:
NHS bosses in England say the way maternity care is organised is "not fit for purpose" with safety at risk, and warn up to 20 smaller units may have to close.
The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, says difficult decisions lie ahead and maternity services need to be consolidated to support safer care.
It said a government taskforce into neonatal and maternity care must tackle key issues such as a lack of specialist staff and a rise in C-sections.
The Department of Health and Social Care said every woman deserves safe maternity care, and the taskforce "will deliver the reforms needed to ensure services meet the needs of women and families now and in the future".
The NHS Alliance said there are particular pressures on smaller units in rural and coastal areas and that those delivering 1,500 to 2,000 babies each year might need to close.
The organisation said up to 20 out of 155 consultant-led maternity units in England face closure. It says staffing problems and rising numbers of C-sections are making smaller units potentially unsafe.
The rise in C-sections was a challenge, according to the NHS Alliance, and there were inadequate operating theatres and beds in outdated and decaying buildings, posing a safety risk.
The NHS leaders' organisation also said some smaller units struggled to maintain safe staffing numbers for 24-hour care, including midwives and consultants such as obstetricians.
It goes on to say the government's taskforce must "grasp the nettle" by tackling these strategic issues, including significantly worse outcomes in deprived communities and raised maternity mortality rates for Black and Asian women.
The director of the NHS Alliance's acute and ambulance network, Matthew Hopkins, said: "Difficult decisions lie ahead, consolidating maternity services to support safer, more sustainable care."
He said any local plans had to involve NHS leaders, clinical staff, patients and communities, and that politicians "must have the courage to make the case for patient safety".
"It is time now to take a step back and consider how we should best organise maternity services across England, and where those services should be located", he said.
The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists called for "other solutions" to be explored that would prevent closing maternity units.
Dr Alison Wright, president of the college said the government should commit to "expanding the maternity workforce to ensure safe staffing levels, along with investment in training and retention of dedicated staff."
"The distinct needs and challenges of smaller units, especially in rural and coastal communities, must be recognised and supported," she added.
In August, a Devon trust suspended standard birthing services at a hospital in Barnstaple leaving pregnant mothers having to make a 53 mile journey to Exeter to give birth.
The Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust said it was the "only safe course of action" due to staffing issues.
The trust added that it had explored every option including locum cover and support from other health organisations but that a temporary suspension was the best solution.
The North Devon maternity facility remains suspended with the trust saying there would be a "readiness assessment" later in October with patient safety the "overriding priority".
Campaigners say the delay is "disappointing". One couple told the BBC the thought of the longer journey for the birth of their second son had left them anxious and angry.
Catherine Mchomvu, chief executive of the Devon Antenatal Family Centre, has been campaigning to secure the future of the Barnstaple facility, and warned that reductions nationally would undermine the quality of care.
"If we had closures of smaller units you are going to find that women are not going to receive any level of continuity of care - that's purely because they are not going to see the same healthcare team more than once throughout the whole antenatal and post-natal experience", she said.
In June, Baroness Valerie Amos's review found women and babies were not being "listened to, heard or believed", with racism and discrimination "embedded throughout the system".

articles.title_orig: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
articles.title_zh: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
articles.content_orig:
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Following some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will on Monday hold a crisis cabinet meeting .
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
Speaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
Student protests that began last month escalated significantly on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

articles.title_orig: What Is The Most Affordable Gaming Console In 2026?
articles.title_zh: What Is The Most Affordable Gaming Console In 2026?
articles.content_orig:
In 2026, the big three gaming industry brands, Microsoft Xbox, Nintendo, and Sony, all have a finger in the pie when it comes to a consumer's decision to buy a console. Sadly economic shifts happen; as a result, gaming has become a luxury not everyone can afford. On paper, Nintendo ties Xbox for the cheapest console to date among the three in the U.S., but it's also the weakest (in terms of hardware), and owning one of its systems comes with hidden costs.
For example, Nintendo first-party titles aren't often on sale — so you're likely coughing up the full price. Secondly, software upgrades aren't always free, as most were with the Xbox Series X, the PlayStation 5, and PlayStation 5 Pro. You usually either pay the Nintendo Switch Online fee — around $20 per year (individual) – or you pay separately for the meaningful ones — around $5 to $20 per game. This isn't terribly pricey, but you can start bleeding out costs if you want the most technically advanced experience with popular Nintendo Switch titles like the "Xenoblade Chronicles" franchise.
Compared to current-gen, the Nintendo Switch 2 costs $500 without a bundle, while the Xbox Series S is priced similarly for the 512 GB edition. The difference is that the Xbox Series S, while still current-gen, is old and digital-only (Microsoft likely incentivizes you to pay for Xbox Game Pass for a more complete experience). The Nintendo Switch 1 would be a fairer comparison; it is still being sold and priced at $230 in 2026. By today's standards, that's the cheapest anyone can get new, even if it is considered last-gen.
The console itself, games, subscriptions, and accessories can drive the costs higher than you'd like. Both Sony and Microsoft charge for expensive online services, which can make Nintendo's $20-a-year look quite appealing. But some of that value is hidden. For example, Sony and Microsoft let you play modern AAA games in their catalogs, and both libraries are expansive. If you take advantage of this, it can save you $60 to $80 per game, which adds up over time.
Nintendo's online membership does have a library of retro games, but none are from the current-gen console. Accessories are another issue. Nintendo may have cheaper consoles, but it doesn't include a premium controller, which arguably offers similar quality to what you'd get from Microsoft and Sony. There's also storage space constraints. The Nintendo Switch 2 uses microSD Express to expand its meager 512GB storage.
The 256GB licensed option costs $60. It's also the only realistic way to expand storage unless you buy cartridges only (not Game-Key Cards) to conserve internal memory. The Xbox Series S and X offer models ranging from 512GB to 2TB (Xbox Series X only), and the PlayStation 5 and all its editions offer a similar range. The difference is that both Xbox and PlayStation 5 offer two ways to expand storage: an external hard drive or an SSD (much more expensive). Lastly, unlike cartridges, game discs on either console need to transfer and store data internally (on the system) to work.
Retro gaming can be expensive if you are a curated collector. Sadly, that means limited editions and unopened console systems can be priced through the roof. For example, the Nintendo GameCube (regular edition) is quite affordable used, around $100, but the Japanese-only Panasonic Q GameCube costs well over a grand ($1,654 for the core console). You can also find pre-owned consoles through online marketplaces.
A PlayStation 2 on eBay can cost anywhere from just under $100 to a bit over $200, depending on condition and what it comes with. The tricky part is finding games, since retro gaming predates the digital storefront era , so you will need a working disc or cartridge to play them. Some games are harder to find than others; a copy of "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness" can cost more than the console itself. That might seem daunting, but the used market is still vast, and if you are lucky to be near one, GameStop Retro specializes in selling retro hardware .

articles.title_orig: This Pocket-Sized Multitool Is An Affordable Leatherman Alternative
articles.title_zh: This Pocket-Sized Multitool Is An Affordable Leatherman Alternative
articles.content_orig:
Not every job calls for an entire crew armed to the teeth with a bunch of tools. Sometimes, for stuff like a loose bolt, a one-size-fits-all solution works best – like a pocket multitool . Here, people typically go for Leatherman, a company that claims to have built the first pliers-based multitool. Among its offerings, the Leatherman Wave+, a full-size multi-tool, is one of the most popular options in its category.
Plenty of Leatherman rivals try to undercut these offerings on price, but one of the more interesting upcoming options comes from Tsuchioto Works, a Tokyo design studio. It's called the Blackjaw, a pocket-sized gadget that folds pliers, two blades, a saw, two screwdrivers, two openers, and a carabiner into a single frame. Folded up, it measures just 4.2 inches long and weighs 7.8 ounces. That may be slightly longer than the Wave+, which measures 4 inches, but it's also noticeably lighter at 7.8 ounces versus the 8.5 ounces of the Wave+. It clips to your belt loop with the built-in carabiner, so it's always within reach.
However, the real sell here is the price. The Blackjaw is being sold through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign right now, and the campaign price sits at $90. That's significantly lower than the $129.95 tag on the Wave+. Shipping to the U.S. adds another $15, but even with it, you're still only at $105. You can also further knock off a few bucks with the Super Early Bird tier, taking the price down to around $80. That said, Tsuchioto plans to charge $119 once the campaign ends. Unfortunately, backers will have to wait a while to actually get the product since Tsuchioto doesn't expect to start shipping the Blackjaw until March 2027.
Price aside, the biggest difference between the Blackjaw and the Wave+ is that none of the parts on the Blackjaw are detachable. Having no detachable parts means you won't accidentally lose a set of bits, meaning to can complete a job. The downside, however, is that the tool is left with just two drivers, a Phillips and a flathead.
As for the Blackjaw itself, the name pretty much spells out the design. The tool is essentially a pair of plier jaws with two handles, with almost the whole thing wearing a matte black finish. While the handles are aluminum, the blades, jaws, and drivers are made of stainless steel. Since every implement here folds out from the outer side of the two handles, you can use the blade or driver without first having to unfold the pliers.
All in all, you get 11 tools on the Blackjaw, including that carabiner. There's the plier head designed to stack long-nose tips for small parts, a toothed jaw for nuts and pipe, and a wire cutter. Then there's the double-sided saw for handling small branches and dowels. The can and bottle openers cover meals at the camp. A separate notch is designed for stripping wire. Finally, the knife is designed for boxes and cord. So overall, it's a complete tool that can handle a lot of jobs, and undercuts its chief competitor in price by a fair bit.

Happy Friday, traders. Welcome to our weekly market wrap, where we take a look back at these last five trading days with a focus on the market news, economic data, and headlines that had the most impact on gold prices and other key correlated assets—and may continue to in the future.
So, what kind of week has it been?
Gold recovered to around $4,175/oz by Friday morning after touching a weekly low near $4,080, leaving it slightly below its opening levels for the week.
Hotter-than-expected September CPI and PPI data initially pressured the non-yielding metal as traders considered the possibility of additional interest rate hikes.
Gold then rallied as inflation concerns weighed on stocks and the US Dollar Index softened, suggesting investors were looking beyond interest rate expectations alone.
Next week's lighter macro calendar will test whether this broader risk-off mood persists ahead of the following week's FOMC decision.
Despite a deep dip in the middle of the chart, this week feels like the first time in quite a while that gold has flexed its muscle as the market's historical preference for safe-haven hedging against elevated inflation. A double shot of key inflation data for the US economy came in notably hotter than expected. Based on the last 12 months of trading, that is exactly the kind of news we would expect to crush the yellow metal as a non-yielding asset, given that the traditional monetary policy response would be to raise interest rates again.
And certainly, gold prices dropped sharply on Wednesday morning. But as markets more fully digested the data, the more tangible risk of painfully elevated inflation became investors' key concern, outweighing projections of higher interest rates in the medium term. As a result, traders and managers stepped back into gold positions on Thursday and Friday and managed to push spot prices back to $4,175/oz—still a decrease for the week, but within touching distance of Sunday's opening marks.
Market consensus projections for this week's inflation data were far from expecting any pullback in the recent reacceleration of consumer and manufacturing prices, but the numbers released on Wednesday and Thursday came in even higher. Core CPI came in 0.1 percentage point above expectations on a year-over-year basis, as did the headline inflation figure, which was powered by a 9.1% surge in gasoline prices in September.
More concerning for the future path of consumer inflation, September PPI, a measure of prices received by domestic producers, rose 1.3% month over month—an eye-watering 80 basis points above the consensus estimate. In the immediate reaction to the CPI print, spot gold shed nearly $100/oz, falling to a weekly low of $4,080. While there was a modest bounce off the floor, it looks as though the ugly PPI data really kicked investors' fears into overdrive, helping fuel gold's sharp rally back to Tuesday's levels.
Our reasoning for assigning a cause to this rebound, rather than chalking it up to coincidence or end-of-week rebalancing, comes from how other asset classes traded at the same time. Following the PPI release, some combination of concern about the darkening threat of higher inflation for longer and the follow-on impact of higher borrowing rates for longer sent US stocks into a broad-based selloff that continued on Friday morning.
The concern about price pressures specifically—not only projected rate hikes—is clearly a key part of the equation here, given that the US Dollar Index softened over the same period. We would expect the dollar to strengthen further if higher rate expectations were the only critical input.
With a relatively quiet week of macro data coming up next and a live FOMC decision the following week, the big question for the immediate trading days ahead will be whether this risk-off swing across multiple asset classes persists or whether something else comes along to superficially improve investors' mood and force gold to once again trade primarily in reaction to interest rate expectations.
In the meantime, traders, I hope you can get out and safely enjoy your weekend for the next couple of days. After that, I'll see you back here next week for another market recap.

articles.title_orig: Indonesian stocks plunge to six-year low as MSCI downgrade fears mount
articles.title_zh: Indonesian stocks plunge to six-year low as MSCI downgrade fears mount
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia's benchmark stock index plunged over 5% on Monday to its lowest level in six years, as concerns over a potential downgrade by MSCI intensified fears of further foreign investor outflows.
The Jakarta Composite Index tumbled to its lowest level since early October 2020, extending a bruising sell-off in Indonesian equities. MSCI, the index provider, on Friday proposed reclassifying Indonesia directly from an emerging market to stand-alone status, raising the prospect of the country's removal from major global equity benchmarks.
MSCI is expected to make a final decision by June, with the potential reclassification hinging on whether Indonesian authorities can demonstrate meaningful improvements in market governance and transparency.
Goldman Sachs warned in a Sunday note that a full removal from MSCI's emerging-market indexes could trigger approximately $5.6 billion in passive fund outflows, equivalent to 18 days of average daily trading volume for constituents of the MSCI Indonesia Investable Market Index.
An additional $2.7 billion could be at risk if FTSE Russell subsequently takes similar action, although the bank stressed that such a move would be a separate scenario.
Goldman estimated that active funds benchmarked to MSCI and FTSE indexes hold more than $8 billion in Indonesian equities, although any selling by these investors would be discretionary rather than automatically triggered by a downgrade.
The bank maintained its underweight rating on Indonesian equities, citing persistent index uncertainty, weak corporate earnings and macroeconomic headwinds.
"Valuations have compressed significantly, but remain above historical troughs; index, earnings, and macro risks constrain a re-rating," Goldman strategists led by Alvin So wrote.
The MSCI Indonesia Index has fallen 47% this year as of Friday, data provided by the bank showed, with foreign investors withdrawing a net $5.1 billion from Indonesian equities over the period.
Foreign ownership of Indonesian stocks has declined to 25% in October from 27% in January, while the value of foreign holdings has nearly halved to approximately $130 billion from $250 billion, the bank said.
Despite the steep declines, Goldman cautioned that Indonesian equities may not have bottomed. The MSCI Indonesia Index's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 7.3 times, its lowest level since the global financial crisis, but remains above historical troughs.
The strategists also expect Indonesia's central bank to raise interest rates twice more, by 25 basis points each in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027, potentially adding further pressure to economic growth and equity valuations.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo Addresses the Faithful a Day After Leaving the Hospital
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo Addresses the Faithful a Day After Leaving the Hospital
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has thanked some 15,000 Catholic faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square during his Sunday address, his first major public appearance since lung cancer surgery.
“Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers,” Leo said.
The 71-year-old pontiff addressed the crowd from a window overlooking the square at the Vatican, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing, he revealed that a nodule had been found in his lung and would be surgically removed.
The operation confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
Leo said the experience of the past week “has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity”.
He told the crowd that he had “truly felt your support” and expressed “particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli Hospital” in Rome, where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa, in Rome for a Catholic meeting, danced and ululated after the pope’s blessing.
“He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of the Congo said. “This is an expression of our joy.”
Meanwhile, Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, United States, said she felt “very blessed” to be present for the pope’s return to his flock.
There had been doubts that a planned papal voyage to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November would go ahead.
The Vatican’s secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told journalists on Friday that the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule “according to the condition of his health”.
But Leo’s surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were “no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead”.
Latin Americans in the crowd in St Peter’s Square welcomed the news.
“We are all hoping for his recovery, and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is OK, and we’re pleased,” Soledad Espinosa from Ecuador said.

articles.title_orig: North Carolina has the lowest gas prices in the country. Some say it's still too high
articles.title_zh: North Carolina has the lowest gas prices in the country. Some say it's still too high
articles.content_orig:
More than a week after North Carolina lawmakers voted to suspend the gas tax, the state now has the lowest gas prices on average in the entire country.
Several people WRAL spoke with on Sunday still aren't satisfied.
“They're still high. Still a lot of money out of my paycheck," gas station customer Hayden Epperson said.
As of Sunday, a gallon of unleaded gas in Raleigh costs an average of $3.62, nearly 35 cents cheaper than a week ago. A gallon of diesel in Raleigh costs $5.62, about 28 cents cheaper than a week ago.
However, it wasn't lost on Epperson just how much lower prices were one year ago. On Oct. 18, 2025, gas cost $2.78 and diesel cost $3.52.
"It's ridiculous. It takes half a tank to get to work. A half tank to get back. And it's not good," Epperson said.
The high costs aren't just affecting commuters driving more than 30 minutes to get to work. Lisa Penny, a farmer's wife who grows produce in Benson, said the high diesel prices are capping off a difficult year for farming.
"Having to buy diesel in bulk has been very, very strenuous and made it hard for us as farmers to keep all the pricing for all of our produce at a low cost," Penny said.
While the gas tax suspension was signed into law on Friday, Oct. 9, it didn't start until days later . Many faced the same prices for days after it was signed. Petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan said there could be a few reasons why.
"It's hard to lower the prices immediately when stations already paid a much higher price for the fuel that's in their tanks," De Haan said. "It takes a few days for them for stations to sell through their existing taxed inventory before they're able to buy the non-taxed fuel. That's why it's taken about a week to to kind of fully realize the the tax suspension."
De Haan said a common misunderstanding about the gas tax he noticed is that gas should be exactly 41 cents lower since the tax suspension was signed into law, but he warned the tax suspension is only one small factor in the price people pay for fuel.
"The tax is suspended, but that doesn't freeze the price of oil from suddenly going up," De Haan said. "The price of oil is moving every day and in the last week it's actually gone up fairly noticeably. This is one of the rare times in my career where beyond a few days out, it's impossible to predict because it's it's not about normal market ebbs and flows right now.
De Haan added that the ongoing war with Iran makes prices extremely volatile, and it's possible they may shoot up again even with the tax out of the picture.
"It's about geopolitical tensions and developments that can happen at a moment's notice," De Haan added. "It depends on what's going on between the US and Iran and Ukraine and Russia."
The gas tax is set to go back in effect December 1.

articles.title_orig: Strait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says
articles.title_zh: Strait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says
articles.content_orig:
International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez discusses efforts to communicate with Tehran as attacks escalate and commercial shipping faces growing risks.
Thousands of sailors remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks on commercial ships, the United Nations' top maritime official warned Sunday after Iran accused the U.S. military of using an international emergency radio channel to threaten civilian crews.
The warning also came amid reports that 24 ships had been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, underscoring growing concerns about maritime safety in the region, according to Financial Times .
"The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping," International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.
"There is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS
24 ships have been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, according to reports. (Fatemeh Bahrami / Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict," he warned, adding that his message was not to transit the Strait of Hormuz or put seafarers at risk "until we have guarantees."
Dominguez's warning followed an Oct. 9 letter to the IMO in which Iran alleged that the U.S. military used VHF Channel 16 , an internationally designated maritime distress and safety channel, to intimidate Iranian crews in the Persian Gulf.
"VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf," the letter stated.
TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS
Smoke column rises from tanker El Gaia after incident in the Strait of Hormuz.
"During such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels."
In a statement to Fox News Digital, U.S. Central Command defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports .
"The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners," CENTCOM said.
"Vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply.
"American forces remain highly vigilant, focused, and professional while fully enforcing the naval blockade against Iran ."
Iran's complaint was submitted by Seyed Ali Mousavi, its ambassador to the IMO, and circulated to member states on Oct. 9, according to a copy reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Tehran also accused American forces of turning the maritime safety channel into an "instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews."
The letter cited commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators but provided no recordings, transcripts or specific details of the alleged exchanges. Fox News Digital could not independently verify the accusations.
IRAN THREATENS TO HALT RED SEA TRAFFIC IN RESPONSE TO US MILITARY BLOCKADE OF PORTS
Naval units from Iran simulate the rescue of a hijacked vessel during joint drills at the Port of Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan, Iran, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world," Dominguez said.
"And we have seen this in several parts of the world where Channel 16, that should not be used for this kind of communication, starts receiving messages that may be perceived as actually threatening or that are outside the remit of why it was created."
Iran also asked the IMO to raise its allegations with member states and relevant international organizations, potentially including the International Telecommunication Union.
Dominguez said the IMO could review its regulations and procedures to determine whether stronger safeguards are needed, though he did not announce a formal investigation.
"Our role here at IMO is that when those situations take place, we will then look into any technical measures or any operational aspects that we may need to clarify further within our regulatory framework," he said, stressing that member states have equal rights to raise concerns, regardless of the conflict.
"We have a responsibility, and I have a duty as well, to circulate letters and notes that the countries actually put forward when they're also being affected."
WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS
The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners, CENTCOM said. (U.S. Navy)
"We take all that information, meet at the level of different meetings of the organization and have the discussions," Dominguez added.
"If it's demonstrated that we probably need to improve our rules in order to avoid communications issues, or that we need to enhance the knowledge of how these channels should be used, that is a role for us."
The IMO had recorded 100 confirmed maritime incidents across the region as of Oct. 9, with 24 seafarers killed since the conflict began Feb. 28. Dominguez also warned that fraudulent ship registrations and false flags have become major contributors to the danger.
"What we've also seen right now is an increase in fraudulent registries with false flags that are taking the risk and acting as shuttle tankers in order to bring goods in and out," he said. "That's one of the reasons that we're seeing an escalation.
"And it's the irresponsible shipowners that are taking the risk in order to actually be able to trade and move some of the goods and the cargoes."
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A ship is seen passing through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran on April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
"For me, any single case, any vessel that is attacked, any life of a seafarer that is lost, is a critical situation for me, because they are all relevant, they are all important."
Despite the confrontation, Dominguez said diplomatic channels with Iran remain open, though he has no direct contact with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
"I have communications with all the member states of IMO, and that includes the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.
"Of course, that's through the diplomatic channels. I don't have direct contact with the IRGC .
"I have conversations with them and they respond to my messages. You know, the information flows. What is difficult is to get final decisions because of the conflict that is ongoing."

articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges that she was spying for China
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges that she was spying for China
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has recognized for nearly half a century, though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
articles.title_zh: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.
Writing in the Times newspaper , Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".
"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.
Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".
According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.
In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".
"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.
Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.
"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."
He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".
The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."
Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms.
Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."
Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".
The review's author, former health secretary Alan Milburn, has argued for the need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support" in an interview with the Guardian published on Sunday.
"This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."
Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful" .
Chancellor John Healey, who is due to hand down his first budget on 28 October, told the Labour party conference in September the government had a "moral duty" to address welfare spending.
